description:
We are a group of high school students from Türkiye who share a passion for science, space exploration and technology. Our team comes up with variety of interests and skills including research, creativity and programming. 

We believe that success comes up with curiosity and teamwork. Surprisingly, we have both.
summary: Space agencies invest heavily in terrestrial analog sites to test rovers, habitats, and spacesuits before launch, yet well-characterized analogs for lunar bases and Mars are scarce. Team ERROR 13 built an interactive web-based map and analysis portal that merges NASA, ESA, and USGS data to visualize Earth locations resembling extraterrestrial environments. Our dual-site concept highlights two areas in Türkiye that no analog study has combined before. Plan A, the Nemrut Caldera, serves as a physical and volcanic analog for robotic landing and base planning, letting users explore 3D topography, rover routes, crater-floor base locations, lava flows, and lava tube caves. Plan B, the Lake Van Basin, serves as a chemical and astrobiological analog, comparing its highly alkaline lake chemistry with ancient Martian lake data through charts and biological indicators. By combining two complementary sites in one platform, our portal helps mission planners, engineers, and scientists choose better test sites, avoid costly failures, and prepare for the Moon and Mars faster.
details:
What it does and how it works

TERRA Analog Explorer is an interactive web portal prototype that helps users explore Earth locations that resemble the Moon and Mars. It is built around two complementary sites in Türkiye. Plan A, the Nemrut Caldera in Bitlis, is a physical and volcanic analog for robotic landing and base planning. Plan B, the Lake Van Basin, is a chemical and astrobiological analog.

Users start in a site explorer, choose a research module, and move between connected screens:

  • Mission planner (Nemrut): a topographic map with sample rover routes, candidate base locations, lava flow layers, lava tube candidates, a route elevation profile, and a Mars/Moon target switch.
  • Astrobiology (Lake Van): side-by-side charts comparing alkaline lake chemistry with a Martian paleolake model, plus a table of life-trace indicators.
  • Surface comparison: NASA imagery of Lake Van beside Jezero Crater on Mars, and Nemrut beside a lunar volcanic terrain, with notes on what can and cannot be compared.
  • Data layers and source library: every layer lists its source and verification status, with links to NASA Moon Trek, Mars Trek, PDS, Mars 2020 and MSL raw images, and Astromaterials 3D.

Benefits and intended impact

Well-characterized analog sites are scarce and expensive to prepare. Our portal gives mission planners, rover engineers, astrobiologists, and planetary scientists a clearer way to compare candidate test sites before committing to costly missions. It also makes the link between Earth terrain and Moon/Mars data easy to understand for students and the public.

Tools and technology

We designed and built the interactive prototype in Figma. Reference imagery and sources come from NASA (ISS astronaut photography, LRO, Mars 2020 Perseverance, Moon Trek, Mars Trek, and PDS). For the next step we plan to connect real data using Python (Pandas, Plotly, Folium), QGIS, the Mapbox API, and NASA, ESA, and USGS datasets. The prototype interface is currently in Turkish, and an English version is planned.

How it is creative

Most analog studies focus on well-known deserts such as Atacama or Utah. We combine a volcanic site (Nemrut) and an alkaline lake (Lake Van) in one dual-site concept, covering both the physical and the chemical-astrobiological side of exploration within a single workflow, in one region.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: Maps and values in the prototype are illustrative and clearly labeled. A similarity is not evidence of life, and routes, base locations, and lava tube candidates require field verification.
  • Limits of comparison: Nemrut is volcanic, while lunar craters such as Shackleton are impact craters, so we state what each comparison can and cannot show.
  • Transparency: every layer shows its source and data status, and live data integration is clearly marked as planned.
  • Feasibility: we built a focused prototype that works as a clickable demonstration rather than overpromising unfinished features.
